tunes.title: St. Louis Blues
tunes.form: 12-bar blues strains with a 16-bar habanera section
tunes.summary:
W. C. Handy, the bandleader who called himself the Father of the Blues, published it in 1914, mixing a twelve-bar blues with a strain in the Latin habanera rhythm he'd heard in Cuba and on Memphis dance floors. It became one of the most recorded songs of the first half of the century.

The tango section is the thing to listen for: some versions keep it, some swing straight through it, and it tells you how each band hears the Caribbean in the blues.

versions.note: Just voice, Louis Armstrong's cornet and a reed organ: Armstrong answers each line as if he were a second singer.
From Louis Armstrong Plays W. C. Handy: nearly nine minutes with his All Stars and Velma Middleton, taking every strain, the tango section included, at an easy rolling tempo.

versions.title: Boogie Woogie On St. Louis Blues
versions.note: Hines turns it into a boogie-woogie piano showpiece, the left hand rolling eight to the bar.
From Gershwin's World, with Stevie Wonder singing and playing harmonica over a loose, modern groove: the old tune heard through soul music.

tunes.title: Body and Soul
tunes.form: AABA, 32 bars (the bridge moves up a half step)
tunes.summary:
A torch song from a 1930 Broadway revue, it became the ballad every saxophonist is measured against after Coleman Hawkins recorded it in 1939 and barely played the melody at all.

Its chords move in unexpected directions, especially in the bridge, which is why players treat it as a test: listen for how each version gets through the bridge and back.

versions.note: Two choruses of improvisation that hint at the melody only in the first bars, then build to a climax: a hit record made of pure invention.
Holiday sings the words Hawkins left out, slightly behind the beat, turning the torch song into something private.
Solo piano on Monk's Dream: the melody stated plainly, then knocked off balance with his dissonant fills and stride left hand.
Coltrane reharmonises it with his own moving chords and plays it as a slow, searching ballad over McCoy Tyner and Elvin Jones.

tunes.title: Stardust
tunes.summary:
Hoagy Carmichael first recorded it as a medium-tempo instrumental in 1927, inspired, he said, by the cornet of his friend Bix Beiderbecke. Slowed down and given Mitchell Parish's lyric in 1929, it became one of the most recorded songs of the century.

The melody wanders like an improvised solo, which is why players love it: listen for who keeps the long verse and who goes straight to the refrain.

versions.note: Armstrong rewrites the melody as he sings it, repeating and bending phrases, then plays it the same free way on trumpet.
The big-band hit: strings, a sumptuous arrangement and Shaw's clarinet soaring over it.
From the Just Jazz concert in Pasadena: a jam session where each soloist takes the tune somewhere, Hampton's vibes last.
Cole sings the rarely heard verse in full before the refrain, over Gordon Jenkins's strings.
The country singer's album of standards made it a hit again: sparse, conversational, close to how Carmichael first heard it.

tunes.title: I Got Rhythm
tunes.summary:
Written for the 1930 musical Girl Crazy, where Ethel Merman stopped the show with it. Its chord sequence, rhythm changes, became the second most common structure in jazz after the blues: countless bebop tunes are new melodies written over it.

Listen for the bridge's chain of dominant chords, a moment every soloist has to navigate at speed.

versions.note: A hot band record a year after the show: Armstrong hands the tune around the band before taking it home.
At the 1938 Carnegie Hall concert the quartet, with Teddy Wilson, Lionel Hampton and Gene Krupa, takes it fast and light: chamber jazz from the first famous integrated small group.
From her Gershwin Songbook, with Nelson Riddle: the lyric sung with clear delight, the swing light and exact.

tunes.title: Summertime
tunes.summary:
A lullaby from Gershwin's opera Porgy and Bess, sung in the first scene. Short, in a minor key and built on a few chords, it has been recorded tens of thousands of times, by jazz players, soul singers and rock bands.

Because there's so little to it, each version is mostly the performer: listen for the tempo and the bass line, which change the song more than any reharmonisation.

versions.note: A year after the opera opened, Holiday swings it at medium tempo: a lullaby turned into a small-band jazz record.
Bechet's soprano saxophone, with its wide vibrato, sings the melody almost operatically. It was one of Blue Note's first hits.
Arranged by Russell Garcia as a duet: Ella's clarity and Louis's gravel trading lines over strings.
Gil Evans's orchestra repeats a soft figure while Miles plays muted trumpet over it: the whole tune hovers.
Fast and modal, with Coltrane's sheets of sound pouring over a single chord: the lullaby barely survives, on purpose.

tunes.title: Caravan
tunes.summary:
Ellington's Puerto Rican valve trombonist Juan Tizol brought the melody; Ellington shaped it into the band's exotic showpiece. It was one of the first Latin-tinged jazz standards, years before the Afro-Cuban craze.

The A sections hang over one chord while the drums keep a tom-tom pattern; the bridge suddenly swings. Listen for how each band handles that switch.

versions.note: The orchestra version: Tizol's trombone states the snaking melody over tom-toms, then the band swings the bridge.
From Monk's album of Ellington tunes: the melody played straight but voiced with his crunched, angular chords.
From Money Jungle, a trio with Charles Mingus and Max Roach: tense, percussive, almost violent, three generations pushing each other.
The Jazz Messengers with Freddie Hubbard and Wayne Shorter: a hard bop flag-waver with Blakey's drums driving the vamp.

tunes.title: Cherokee
tunes.summary:
An English bandleader's song, written as part of an 'Indian Suite', it became the young bebop musicians' test piece: a long form, a bridge that moves through distant keys, and tempos that get faster every year.

Charlie Parker said he found his way into bebop while working through its chords in 1939. Listen for the bridge: at speed, it separates the players who know the changes from the ones who don't.

versions.note: The swing-era hit, at a comfortable dance tempo: the melody the boppers would later take apart.

versions.title: Ko Ko
versions.note: Parker's new tune over Cherokee's chords at a breakneck tempo, with Max Roach and Dizzy Gillespie on trumpet: a manifesto for bebop.
From Study in Brown: Brown's trumpet runs through the bridge with a clarity and warmth that made it look easy.

tunes.title: All the Things You Are
tunes.summary:
From a Broadway flop, Very Warm for May, it outlived the show by decades. Its chords travel through five keys in thirty-six bars, so it became the standard musicians call to show they can follow a long harmonic road.

Listen for the introduction the boppers added, and for how players handle the turn at the end of the bridge.

versions.note: Dizzy's and Bird's version opened with a new introduction that later players kept: bebop claiming a show tune as its own.
From her Jerome Kern Songbook: sung as a ballad with Nelson Riddle, so you can hear how lovely the melody is.
The trio with Gary Peacock and Jack DeJohnette that took standards seriously again: long, singing lines and constant interplay.

tunes.title: How High the Moon
tunes.summary:
A ballad from a 1940 revue that bebop musicians played so fast and so often it became their anthem. Its chords also carry Charlie Parker's Ornithology, so the two are often heard back to back.

Listen for the tempo first: from ballad to dance band to scat to guitar trickery, the same chords take every speed.

versions.note: The swing-era version, the same year as the show: a bright dance tempo and Goodman's clarinet.
A number one pop hit built from multi-tracked guitars and voices in Les Paul's home studio: jazz changes, new technology.
Live in Berlin: nearly seven minutes of scat, quoting one tune after another, never losing the chords.

tunes.title: Take the "A" Train
tunes.summary:
Billy Strayhorn wrote it from Ellington's directions to his house, which began with taking the A train uptown to Harlem. Recorded in 1941, it became the Ellington orchestra's theme.

Listen for the raised fourth note in the melody's second bar, the touch that gives it its lift, and for the train-like brass in the last chorus.

versions.note: The original, with Ray Nance's trumpet solo, first muted, then open: compact and perfectly paced.
From her Duke Ellington Songbook, with Ellington's own band: Ella scats her way through it.
From Ellington Uptown: Betty Roché sings it slow, then double-time with a bebop scat chorus, over the full band.

tunes.title: A Night in Tunisia
tunes.form: AABA, 32 bars, with an interlude and a break
tunes.summary:
Dizzy Gillespie wrote it in 1942 while playing with Benny Carter's band, mixing a Latin bass line in the A sections with swing in the bridge. The interlude ends with a four-bar break, a silence the soloist has to fill alone.

Listen for that break: it's the moment each version is remembered for.

versions.note: The composer's own small band: the Latin vamp, then Dizzy's high, fast trumpet in the break.
On the famous Dial take, Parker's four-bar alto break is so dense the label issued it on its own as 'The Famous Alto Break'.
Blakey opens with a long drum feature, and the band with Lee Morgan and Wayne Shorter turns it into eleven minutes of fire.
Retitled 'And the Melody Still Lingers On', with Dizzy himself on trumpet and lyrics over a funk groove.
versions.record: What Cha' Gonna Do for Me

tunes.title: 'Round Midnight
tunes.summary:
Monk wrote it as a young man; Cootie Williams, who recorded it first in 1944, took a co-composer credit. It's the most recorded jazz original by a jazz musician.

Listen for the introduction and ending: Dizzy Gillespie's band added a coda that almost everyone has kept since, and Miles Davis's version made the tune famous with it.

versions.note: The first recording, by Williams's big band with a young Bud Powell on piano: lush and slow.
Monk's own first recording, for Blue Note: the melody with his wrong-sounding right notes, exactly as he meant it.
Muted trumpet on the melody, then the band's sudden fanfare interlude and Coltrane's tenor: the version that made the tune famous.

tunes.title: Autumn Leaves
tunes.summary:
A French song, 'Les feuilles mortes', written for a 1946 film, with an English lyric by Johnny Mercer in 1947. Its chords move in plain circles of fourths through a major key and its relative minor, which makes it the first standard many students learn.

Listen for the long introduction on Cannonball's record, and for how Bill Evans's trio passes the melody around.

versions.note: The English lyric, sung warmly and simply: the version that made it a standard in America.
From Somethin' Else: a long, brooding vamp introduction, then Miles Davis's muted trumpet on the melody.
From Portrait in Jazz: piano, bass and drums trading lines as equals, Scott LaFaro's bass as much a voice as the piano.
A long live performance by the Standards trio that grows from the tune into a gospel-tinged vamp.

tunes.title: My Funny Valentine
tunes.summary:
From the 1937 musical Babes in Arms, a love song that teases its subject. In the 1950s Chet Baker made it his and, through him, the West Coast's; then Miles Davis turned it into something stormier.

Listen for the descending line under the opening phrase, a slow chromatic fall that every arrangement keeps.

versions.note: Sung softly and almost without vibrato, the trumpet's tone in his voice: the version that made him a star.
From her Rodgers and Hart Songbook: the lyric's wit and tenderness both, unhurried.
Live with Herbie Hancock, Ron Carter and Tony Williams: fifteen minutes in which the band speeds up, stops and starts again.

tunes.title: My Favorite Things
tunes.summary:
A cheerful list song from The Sound of Music. A year after the show opened, John Coltrane recorded it on soprano saxophone as a long modal vamp in waltz time, and a Broadway tune became one of the signature pieces of 1960s jazz.

Listen for how much time Coltrane spends on just two chords, and how the waltz never stops turning.

versions.note: The original Broadway cast: bright, brisk and short, the song Coltrane started from.
Fourteen minutes on soprano saxophone over McCoy Tyner's rocking chords and Elvin Jones's waltz.
Live at Newport, with Roy Haynes on drums: longer, wilder, Coltrane pushing the vamp toward ecstasy.
The film soundtrack, the version most people know: a reminder of the simple melody underneath.

tunes.title: Take Five
tunes.summary:
Paul Desmond wrote it for the Dave Brubeck Quartet's Time Out, an album of unusual meters. A tune in five beats to the bar became the best-selling jazz single of its time.

Listen to Joe Morello's drums: the solo is built over a vamp that never loses count.

versions.note: Desmond's dry, light alto over Brubeck's two-chord vamp, and Morello's drum solo in five.
With Brubeck's quartet and a new lyric: proof the odd meter can be sung.
Live, scatting and singing in five over a funk rhythm section: the vocal athletics the tune invites.

tunes.title: The Girl from Ipanema
tunes.summary:
Jobim and the poet Vinícius de Moraes wrote 'Garota de Ipanema' about a girl they saw walking to the beach. Recorded by Stan Getz and João Gilberto, with Astrud Gilberto singing the English words, it made bossa nova a worldwide craze.

Listen for the bridge, which drifts through faraway keys before landing back home as if nothing happened.

versions.note: João sings in Portuguese, Astrud in English, Getz's tenor floats over the guitar's bossa rhythm.
Sinatra sings softly, almost whispering, with Jobim's guitar and voice and Claus Ogerman's strings.
From her Antonio Carlos Jobim Songbook, late in her career: bossa nova sung with a jazz singer's swing.

tunes.title: Footprints
tunes.summary:
Wayne Shorter's minor blues with a twist: it's in six, and its turnaround uses unexpected chords. He recorded it first on his own Adam's Apple, and the same year with Miles Davis's quintet.

Listen to the bass ostinato that holds everything down while the rhythm section stretches time around it.

versions.note: The composer's quartet with Herbie Hancock: a calm, almost mysterious statement of the tune.
From Miles Smiles: Tony Williams pulls the 6/4 into four and back, the time breathing under the solos.
From Footprints Live!, with Danilo Pérez, John Patitucci and Brian Blade: the tune opened up, barely stated, all interplay.

tunes.title: Blue Monk
tunes.summary:
A twelve-bar blues with a melody that climbs in small steps, as if Monk were testing each note before trusting it. It's one of his most played tunes, simple enough for a jam session and full of his quirks.

Listen for the half-step neighbour notes in the melody: they're what make it unmistakably Monk.

versions.note: The first recording, a trio with Percy Heath and Art Blakey: the theme stated with deliberate, spaced-out phrasing.
Monk sitting in with Blakey's Jazz Messengers, Johnny Griffin's tenor taking it fast and hard.
Lincoln wrote and sang words for it on Straight Ahead: a blues about the blues, sung with grit.

tunes.title: Straight, No Chaser
tunes.summary:
A blues built on one short phrase repeated and shifted so it lands on a different beat each time, a Monk trick that makes a simple line sound unpredictable.

Listen for where the phrase falls against the beat: Monk placed it so it never quite settles.

versions.note: The Blue Note original, with Milt Jackson on vibes: the phrase tossed back and forth across the bar lines.
From Milestones, with Coltrane and Cannonball Adderley: a fast, swinging blowing session on Monk's theme.
The title track of his late Columbia album: the quartet with Charlie Rouse, relaxed and sure of itself.

tunes.title: Lonely Woman
tunes.form: Free form around a written lament
tunes.summary:
The opening track of The Shape of Jazz to Come: a mournful melody that floats over a fast, restless rhythm section, two tempos at once. It made Ornette Coleman's revolution sound beautiful.

Listen for the difference between the slow, crying horns and the drums racing underneath.

versions.note: Alto and Don Cherry's cornet in a slightly ragged unison, over Billy Higgins's brisk drums and Charlie Haden's bass drone.
versions.record: The Shape of Jazz to Come

versions.note: The most elegant band in jazz plays the free-jazz anthem as chamber music, with Milt Jackson's vibes.
Ornette's old bandmates, Don Cherry, Dewey Redman, Charlie Haden and Ed Blackwell, revisit it twenty years on: slower, darker, a lament among friends.

tunes.title: Afro Blue
tunes.form: Minor modal theme over 6/8 and 3/4 at once
tunes.summary:
Mongo Santamaría's tune was one of the first jazz standards built on an Afro-Cuban rhythm in three, the 6/8 bell pattern heard against a 3/4 bass line. John Coltrane's quartet turned it into one of its ecstatic live pieces.

Listen for the two meters running at once: the bass in three, the percussion in six.

versions.note: The original, on flute and congas: light, hypnotic and rooted in Cuban rhythm.
From Abbey Is Blue, with Oscar Brown Jr.'s words: a dream of Africa sung over the 6/8 groove.
Live at Birdland on soprano saxophone: Elvin Jones turns the rhythm into a storm.
From Black Radio, with Erykah Badu singing over a slow, hip-hop-tinged groove.

tunes.title: Watermelon Man
tunes.summary:
Herbie Hancock wrote it about the watermelon sellers' cart he remembered from Chicago, and recorded it on his first album, Takin' Off. A year later Mongo Santamaría's Latin version became a pop hit; a decade after that Hancock remade it as funk.

One tune, three grooves: listen for what each band does with the bass line.

versions.note: The original, a gospel-tinged hard bop groove with Freddie Hubbard and Dexter Gordon.
Congas and a cha-cha-style groove: the version that reached the pop charts.
From Head Hunters: Bill Summers blowing into a beer bottle, then a slow funk groove with synthesizers.

tunes.title: In a Sentimental Mood
tunes.summary:
One of Ellington's most tender ballads, recorded by his orchestra in 1935. It moves between minor and major, which gives its melody a wistful, unresolved feel.

Listen for the first notes of the bridge, where the tune suddenly turns bright before slipping back into the minor.

versions.note: The orchestra's original: the melody passed among the saxophones, sweet and a little melancholy.
Ellington's piano introduction, then Coltrane's tenor singing the melody with total calm: one of the most loved ballad recordings in jazz.
From her Duke Ellington Songbook: the ballad sung slowly and plainly, letting the melody's turns between minor and major do the work.

tunes.title: Lover Man
tunes.summary:
A ballad written with Billie Holiday in mind, and she made it a hit in 1945. The following year Charlie Parker recorded it on a day he was so ill he could barely stand, a performance he later wished had never been released.

Listen for how each singer or player stretches the line 'Oh where can you be?'.
aliases: Lover Man (Oh, Where Can You Be?)

versions.note: Her Decca hit with strings: longing sung without self-pity, the phrasing slightly behind the beat.
With Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker: the young Vaughan's voice already rich and sure, bebop horns behind her.
The Dial session recorded the night he collapsed: unsteady and painfully moving.

tunes.title: Goodbye Pork Pie Hat
tunes.summary:
Mingus's elegy for Lester Young, who had died a few weeks before the session and was known for his pork pie hat. It's a slow blues with chords nobody else would put under one.

Listen for the long, sighing melody played in unison by the saxophones.

versions.note: From Mingus Ah Um: John Handy's tenor carries the lament over the band's slow, dragging beat.
From Wired: the rock guitarist plays it with sustain and bends, a sign of how far the tune travelled.
From Mingus, her collaboration with the dying bassist, with her own lyrics about Lester Young and the city.

tunes.title: Night and Day
tunes.summary:
Cole Porter wrote it for Fred Astaire in the 1932 musical Gay Divorce. The melody repeats one note insistently before breaking into a long phrase, like the obsession the lyric describes.

Listen for that repeated note at the start, and what each performer does with it.

versions.note: The original, sung lightly with a dance band: elegant and conversational.
The Quintette of the Hot Club of France swings it on strings, Stéphane Grappelli's violin and Django's guitar trading.
From her Cole Porter Songbook: the verse and the refrain, sung with perfect diction.
From Everybody Digs Bill Evans: a trio version that turns the tune's insistence into rhythmic play.

tunes.title: Lush Life
tunes.summary:
Billy Strayhorn began writing it as a teenager in Pittsburgh: a world-weary song about cocktail lounges and lost love, with wandering harmonies and a lyric full of worldliness he hadn't yet lived. It wasn't recorded until 1949.

Listen for the verse: it's as long as the refrain, and singers who skip it miss half the song.

versions.note: The first well-known recording, with strings: smooth, a little too sunny for Strayhorn's taste, but it put the song on the map.
An instrumental, with Red Garland: Coltrane's tenor follows the melody's long, unpredictable line.
Hartman's deep baritone with Coltrane's quartet: many think it the definitive vocal version.

tunes.title: Manteca
tunes.summary:
Chano Pozo, a Cuban percussionist already famous at home, joined Dizzy Gillespie's big band in 1947 on Mario Bauzá's recommendation and brought him the idea for this tune. Pozo wrote the layered Afro-Cuban figures of the introduction and the A sections, Gillespie the bridge, and Gil Fuller the horn lines. Pozo was killed in Harlem the next year, but Manteca became one of the first Latin jazz standards.

Listen for the change at the bridge: the Cuban vamp gives way to sixteen bars of swing (Gillespie said he meant to write eight), and every version decides how hard to mark the switch.

versions.note: The first recording, by the big band in December 1947: Pozo's conga and the bass set up the groove, and the horns stack riffs on top of it, layer by layer.

versions.title: Manteca Theme
versions.note: The opening of a four-part suite Chico O'Farrill arranged for an enlarged orchestra on Afro: the same theme, rescored with more brass and a full Latin percussion section.
A piano trio with Ray Barretto added on congas: the big-band riffs turned into Garland's block chords, with the conga keeping the Cuban feel underneath.
Half a century on, a big band led from the drums by Bobby Sanabria, from Afro-Cuban Dream: Live & In Clave!!!, with the percussion section as loud as the brass.

tunes.title: Misty
tunes.summary:
Erroll Garner said he thought of it on a flight to Chicago, watching a rainbow through the haze as the plane came down, and recorded it as a piano piece in July 1954. Johnny Burke added the words a few years later, and singers took it up.

Listen to how the melody falls and climbs back in every phrase. Garner's right hand lags a little behind the beat while his left keeps a steady, guitar-like strum.

versions.note: The first recording, with Wyatt Ruther on bass and Fats Heard on drums: the melody in thick, ringing chords, the left hand keeping an even, guitar-like pulse.
Recorded in Paris in July 1958 with an orchestra and strings arranged by Quincy Jones, and issued on a single with Broken Hearted Melody in 1959.
The pop hit: Mathis's high, gentle tenor with an orchestra arranged by Glenn Osser. It reached No. 12 in the US and became his signature song.
Live in Berlin in February 1960 with Paul Smith's quartet, at the same concert as her Mack the Knife.

tunes.title: So What
tunes.form: AABA, 32 bars: D Dorian, with the bridge a half step up
tunes.summary:
The opening track of Kind of Blue, recorded in March 1959. Instead of chords that change every bar or two, there are only two scales: sixteen bars of D Dorian, eight a half step higher, then D again. The bass plays the theme, and the band answers each phrase with a two-chord figure, 'so what', voiced by Bill Evans in stacked fourths.

With so little harmony to follow, the soloists have to make the shape themselves. Listen for how the tempo rose over the years: the band played it faster and faster on stage.

versions.note: Paul Chambers states the theme on bass, the horns answer with the two-chord figure, and Davis's solo leaves a lot of space.
Live at the Olympia in Paris in March 1960, on Coltrane's last tour with the band, with Wynton Kelly on piano: much faster than the record, and over thirteen minutes long.
The second quintet at Philharmonic Hall in New York, with Herbie Hancock, Ron Carter, Tony Williams and George Coleman: even faster than in 1960.
Eddie Jefferson, credited as an innovator of vocalese, sings a lyric by Christopher Acemandese Hall over the tune, with James Moody in the band.

tunes.title: Giant Steps
tunes.form: 16 bars, moving between three keys a major third apart
tunes.summary:
John Coltrane recorded it in May 1959 for the album of the same name. The chords move through B, G and E-flat major, a new key every bar or two, joined by quick two-five-one progressions; players still practise it as a test.

Listen to the pianist on the original: Tommy Flanagan, given the tune with little preparation, plays a halting, stop-start solo. Every later version is partly an answer to how hard the changes are.

versions.note: Coltrane runs the changes at full speed, chorus after chorus, and Flanagan gets through his solo in short, careful phrases.
A big-band arrangement, from a Woody Herman album named for the tune that won a Grammy in 1974.
Twenty-three years later Flanagan made a whole album of Coltrane's tunes in his memory, with George Mraz and Al Foster, and this time plays the tune as the leader.
From the debut album of a pianist from Bali, released when he was eleven. It earned him a Grammy nomination for best improvised jazz solo.

tunes.title: Naima
tunes.summary:
Coltrane's ballad for his wife, Juanita Naima Grubbs, recorded for Giant Steps in 1959. He described it as suspended chords over a held E-flat in the bass, with a B-flat underneath the middle section: almost no movement at the bottom, while the chords above shift.

It was the one slow piece on a record of fast ones, and he kept playing it through the 1960s. Listen for how much the band around it changes, from the calm of 1959 to the long live versions of the 1960s.

versions.note: Paul Chambers holds the bass note while the chords move above it. Wynton Kelly takes a short piano solo; Coltrane plays the melody almost without ornament.
Live at the Village Vanguard in May 1966, with Pharoah Sanders, Alice Coltrane and Rashied Ali: fifteen minutes, with a seven-minute solo from Sanders between two shorter ones by Coltrane.
Solo piano, recorded in Tokyo in 1972 for Echoes of a Friend, Tyner's tribute to Coltrane five years after his death: big rolling chords where the band used to be.
A trio version from Flanagan's album in Coltrane's memory, with George Mraz and Al Foster: unhurried, the melody kept close.

tunes.title: Moanin'
tunes.form: AABA, 32 bars, the A sections in call and response
tunes.summary:
Bobby Timmons, the Jazz Messengers' pianist, used to play its opening eight bars between tunes; Benny Golson, the band's tenor player, told him to add a bridge and make it a song. Art Blakey's band recorded it in October 1958 and it gave the record its name.

The A sections are a church call and response: the piano asks, the horns answer. Listen for that exchange, which comes straight from the Black church.

versions.note: Listen to Lee Morgan's trumpet bending notes like a blues singer, and to Timmons's solo, full of gospel chords.
The same band at the Olympia in Paris a few weeks after the studio session, playing the new tune to a European audience.
Jon Hendricks's lyric, sung by the vocal trio: three voices taking the parts the horns played.
versions.record: The Hottest New Group in Jazz

versions.note: The composer's own trio version, with Sam Jones and Jimmy Cobb, from his first album as a leader.

tunes.title: Song for My Father
tunes.summary:
Horace Silver said the rhythm came from a trip to Brazil and the melody from the Cape Verdean folk music he heard from his father. It's four chords, a bass line of roots and fifths, and straight eighth notes rather than swing. Steely Dan borrowed its opening for Rikki Don't Lose That Number in 1974.

On the original, listen to Joe Henderson's tenor solo: he builds it almost entirely from the first three notes he plays, turning them over chorus after chorus.

versions.note: Recorded in October 1964 with Carmell Jones and Joe Henderson: Silver's piano solo first, then Henderson's, built from a three-note idea.
Recorded in Paris for her Horace Silver tribute, with Silver's own words and Silver himself at the piano on this track.
From Shades of Blue, the hip-hop producer Madlib's album made from the Blue Note catalog: a loose, lounge-like version credited to Sound Directions, one of his projects.
Louis Hayes joined Silver's quintet on drums in 1956; sixty years on he made a tribute album, with Gregory Porter singing.

tunes.title: Maiden Voyage
tunes.form: AABA, 32 bars, two suspended chords per section
tunes.summary:
Herbie Hancock first wrote it for a television commercial, for Yardley; the master tape was labelled 'TV Jingle' until it got its name. On the 1965 album it opens the record: a sea-voyage theme over a repeated rhythm that comes from the bossa nova.

The chords are suspended, neither major nor minor, and they don't pull toward a home key. Listen to how the soloists float over them instead of running changes.

versions.note: Freddie Hubbard, George Coleman, Ron Carter and Tony Williams: the rhythm section keeps the ostinato going under the solos, and nobody hurries.
Vibraphone in place of the horns, with Hancock himself on piano, recorded a year after the original for Hutcherson's album Happenings.

versions.title: Maiden Voyage / Everything In Its Right Place
versions.note: Glasper's trio runs it together with Radiohead's Everything in Its Right Place, from the album In My Element.

tunes.title: Nardis
tunes.summary:
Miles Davis wrote it in 1958 for a Cannonball Adderley session and never recorded it himself. Bill Evans, the pianist on that date, took it up and played it for the rest of his life, so often that many assumed he'd written it.

Its scales, the Phrygian dominant and the double harmonic, give it a Spanish or Middle Eastern sound. Listen for how Evans's trios let it grow: from under six minutes in 1961 to twenty-minute performances built around the drums by the end of the decade.

versions.note: The first recording, from Portrait of Cannonball, with Blue Mitchell on trumpet and Bill Evans on piano. Davis wrote it for this session.
With Scott LaFaro and Paul Motian, a few months before LaFaro died: the three instruments trade the lead rather than piano with accompaniment.
Live at the Montreux festival with Eddie Gomez and Jack DeJohnette, the tune stretched out around a drum solo. Madlib sampled this recording for the Madvillain track Raid in 2004.

tunes.title: Stella by Starlight
tunes.summary:
Victor Young wrote the melody for the 1944 ghost film The Uninvited; Ned Washington added words in 1946, and Harry James and Frank Sinatra both had hits with it in 1947. Jazz players liked its long, arching melody and its chords, which keep heading for a key and then turning away.

Listen to the first chord: it isn't the home key, and the song takes a while to settle. Every version has to find its way through that wandering harmony.

versions.note: The first jazz recording, from January 1952, with a large studio orchestra: Parker states the melody and decorates it in quick runs.
The 1958 sextet with Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley and Bill Evans: Davis plays the melody quietly and Evans's chords set the mood.
From Clap Hands, Here Comes Charlie!, with Lou Levy on piano and Herb Ellis on guitar: three minutes, the words sung over a light swing.

versions.artistName: Keith Jarrett, Gary Peacock & Jack DeJohnette
versions.note: Recorded live in Paris in July 1985, the first track of Standards Live: over eleven minutes, the trio taking the old film song a long way from its melody.

tunes.title: On Green Dolphin Street
tunes.form: ABAC, 32 bars: held bass notes alternating with moving chords
tunes.summary:
Bronisław Kaper wrote it for the 1947 film Green Dolphin Street, with Lana Turner. Jazz players picked it up a decade later, first Ahmad Jamal, then Miles Davis, and it has been recorded hundreds of times since.

The tune alternates eight bars over a held bass note with eight bars of fast-moving chords. Listen for the switch between the still sections and the moving ones, and how each band marks it.

versions.note: Ahmad Jamal's trio, from Count 'Em 88: light, spacious, full of pauses. Miles Davis was listening to Jamal's repertoire closely at the time.
The 1958 sextet with Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley and Bill Evans: the version that made it a jazz standard.
From Outward Bound, Dolphy's first album as a leader, with Freddie Hubbard: Dolphy plays bass clarinet, rarely heard as a jazz solo instrument before him, leaping across its range.
Mark Murphy sings the words, from his album Rah!: the critic Ted Gioia's pick among the vocal versions.

tunes.title: Birdland
tunes.form: A chain of riffs over one groove, built up in layers
tunes.summary:
Joe Zawinul named it for the New York club where he'd heard Basie, Armstrong, Ellington and Miles, and where he met his wife; he called it the most important place in his life. Weather Report put it first on Heavy Weather in 1977, and the recording is now in the Grammy Hall of Fame.

There's little improvising: the piece is its arrangement, one riff after another, each added on top of the last until the big theme arrives. Listen for how each new part joins the ones already playing.

versions.note: The bass line, then synthesizer and saxophone riffs piling up until the main theme. Jaco Pastorius said the studio version was a single take.
With a lyric by Jon Hendricks: four voices sing the riffs and the theme. It won a Grammy.
From Back on the Block, with Miles Davis and Dizzy Gillespie on trumpet, James Moody, and Ella Fitzgerald and Sarah Vaughan singing. It won two Grammys.
